An ablation study shows that removing the staging and asking the agent to zero-shot an algorithmic design with a runtime guarantee leads to a copy of the seeded baseline algorithm (random search) or to incomplete proofs. Our study suggests that machine-checked specifications in Lean can replace empirical evaluation in open-ended algorithm discovery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of an automated pipeline that designs efficient black-box optimisation algorithms with machine-checked runtime bounds in Lean.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Self-Supervised Representation Forcing for Few-Step Video Generation
abstract: Few-step distillation is essential for deploying modern video diffusion models. Among existing approaches, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a highly promising paradigm by achieving strong output-space fidelity without adversarial training, while remaining flexible across various student architectures. We observe, however, that DMD fundamentally relies on an output-space objective, lacking explicit regularization on the model's internal representations. As the distillation step count aggressively shrinks, this output-only supervision becomes insufficient, causing the distilled student to degrade in both fine-grained spatial structures and coherent temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce Self Flow Forcing (SF$^2$), which incorporates a predictive representation loss into the DMD framework without altering its output objective. By providing the student and an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teacher with heterogeneous noise levels, we establish an information asymmetry. This formulation forces the student to predict the teacher's internal representations from a more corrupted input, effectively integrating self-supervised representation alignment into distribution matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SF$^2$ effectively mitigates temporal flickering and consistently improves both spatial fidelity and motion quality. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism is architecture-agnostic - seamlessly supporting both bidirectional and causal models - and requires no external feature extractors, introducing minimal computational overhead.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) classifiers commonly rely on a global classification (CLS) token for image-level prediction, which is poorly aligned with local interpretability requirements in medical imaging. We propose SAP-ViT, a Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer that replaces CLS-based classification with direct aggregation of last-layer patch embeddings. This design makes class predictions decomposable into patch-level contributions as part of the forward pass. To encourage concise and readable evidence, SAP-ViT applies sparsity regularization to the patch-weight distribution. Since self-attention mixes information across patch tokens, we further introduce an input-space back-mapping mechanism to estimate which input patches contribute to influential output patch embeddings. We evaluate SAP-ViT qualitatively and quantitatively on multiple medical image classification datasets spanning different imaging modalities. The results show that SAP-ViT maintains strong classification performance while providing consistent and interpretable patch-level explanations across datasets. Ablation results further show that both sparsity regularization and the alignment component of input-space back-mapping contribute to the final explanation quality. Overall, SAP-ViT provides a favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability for ViT-based medical image classification.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
abstract: Linear probes, classifiers that read a language model's internal activations, are widely used to detect harmful requests. They are cheap to train and run, and an auditor who has trained one would like to reuse it when the model is replaced by a successor rather than retrain it for every release. We test how well probes can be reused. For four base models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-32B) we train a probe on the base model with the XSTest prompt set and apply it, unchanged, to two successors of that base: the DeepSeek-R1 distilled reasoning model and the developer's instruction-tuned chat model. We find that the successors rotate the direction separating unsafe from safe prompts by 17$^\circ$ to 35$^\circ$, yet on XSTest the transferred probe's AUC changes by only $-0.011$ to $+0.027$, and on an independent OR-Bench evaluation, never used for training, by $-0.015$ to $+0.053$. On XSTest, whose safe prompts deliberately contain alarming words, the probes beat a classifier that sees only the prompt text by 0.15 to 0.20 AUC. On the OR-Bench prompts that margin shrinks to 0.03 to 0.20, and the probes flag 29\% to 42\% of prompts that sound harmful but are benign, so part of what they read is the appearance of harm rather than harm itself. A probe trained on a base model can thus be reused, in these families, after distillation and after instruction tuning; how much it reads beyond textual cues depends on the test set.

title: Distributed Predictive Flocking for a Swarm of Miniature Vibration-Driven Robots in a Confined Arena
abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.

title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
abstract: A full-duplex spoken dialogue model must yield when the user cuts in and hold when the user merely backchannels. Sequence-level RL with a timing reward (GRPO) is the usual recipe; we test its whole-rollout form on four open models and find two failures. A binary window reward gives zero advantage on exactly the windows that most need learning (a zero-gradient trap), and the one score per rollout is spread over listening-state decisions the reward is not written in terms of (credit leakage), so the model talks into silence or stops answering. Both come from sampling a reward that is a known function of a few binary control decisions. We propose \emph{window likelihood} (\WL): sample a continuation per window, but integrate in closed form over the stop decisions it visits and maximise the log-probability of acting correctly---a noisy-OR for yielding, a survival product for holding. On HumDial-FDBench, \WL\ gives the best yield/hold F1 on all six structurally different open models we post-train, exceeds Kyutai's released GRPO checkpoints (trained on different data), and adds no re-opening of the floor on any model.

title: Hyperspectral Unmixing using a Structured Linear Mixing Model with Additive Spectral Variability
abstract: Linear hyperspectral unmixing aims at retrieving pure material spectra present in an observed scene and their associated abundance fractions in each pixel. In most practical situations, hyperspectral images are affected by spectral variability (SV) also known as intra-class variability, which is caused by different physical phenomena including atmospheric effects, intrinsic variability of the pure materials and illumination or topographic changes. Nevertheless, the standard hyperspectral unmixing methods that rely on the Linear Mixing Model (LMM) do not consider these phenomena. Thus, neglecting them will spread errors throughout the linear hyperspectral unmixing process. To avoid this problem, this paper proposes two hyperspectral unmixing algorithms dedicated to a parametric model called Structured Additive Variability LMM (SAV-LMM). This mixing model handles SV in an additive manner by incorporating two terms into the standard LMM. Moreover, the designed algorithms are based on Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and optimize a cost function which integrates additional penalization accounting for SV. Furthermore, a novel improved initialization scheme, which takes SV into account, is proposed. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for linearly unmixing hyperspectral images with SV compared to the tested state-of-the-art methods.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
abstract: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent that we use for research on problems whose answers aprogram or data can check. Each candidate solution is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox; proposers see only a public score, and a private split decides what counts. The harness itself(prompts, tools, skills, playbook, meta agent) is an editable genome, changed only through a kernel-enforced gate with held-out and cost checks. An autonomous mode goes from a plain-text goal to a verified report with no human step: an agent picks an open problem and writes its verifier, the kernel calibrates it, an adversarial agent audits it, and an agent that never sees the verifier re-checks the result. Across fourteen problems in six days, for about $180 of model usage, the system produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information: a certified depolarizing-channel threshold point p = 0.064966, a qutrit positivity frontier of 0.2910672, a 44-gate depth-6 Golay state preparation, and a stabilizer-rank bound chi(T^7) <= 10. It also cut SABRE qubit-routing overhead from 68,559 to 12,087 added gates. In hardware, it cut the energy per MAC of an open 8x8 INT8 systolic tile by 77.7% through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow, bit-exact. Three fully autonomous runs ended in honestties with public records; one audit caught a stale record, and one agent-written score pointing the wrong way went unnoticed. We report the failures as carefully: the one self-derived harness generation was rejected on cost, proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and operator changes were decisive for several results.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
abstract: We introduce ExCal, a normal-only multivariate time series anomaly detector that combines raw state retrieval, a signal/derivative subspace, and robust statistics across temporal scales. Each expert map receives a high normality floor from the training prefix. During scoring, positive excess is retained, attenuated for broadly firing maps, and combined with a small rank term. The method fits reference memories and projections without gradient optimization or anomaly labels. Prevalence and ranks depend on the complete scored sequence, making inference batch and transductive rather than online. On 180 series from 17 TSB-AD-M families, ExCal obtains AUC-PR $0.421\pm0.37$ and VUS-PR $0.452\pm0.37$ over three seeds, ranking second among 24 methods. Holm-adjusted paired tests detect no significant difference from AxonAD or StreamVAE, which are the two leading non-pretrained methods on TSB-AD-M, on either primary metric, while finding significant positive differences against the other 21 baselines. A separate single-run probe over three series measures median model-wrapper time of $0.0662$ s. Ablations associate the largest primary-metric changes with raw retrieval and excess-magnitude preservation. The evaluated score is decomposable by expert, but its diagnostic utility and online suitability remain untested.

title: Copying As Defense: Protecting Images from Editing By Eliciting Model Copying
abstract: Image editors built on diffusion transformers (DiTs), such as Flux Kontext, make it possible to turn a single photograph into a convincing manipulated image, including harmful and non-consensual edits. Proactive defenses aim to prevent such manipulations by adding an imperceptible perturbation before an image is shared. Existing defenses for DiT-based in-context editors make the output attend less to the protected reference image. But this leaves the model free to follow the edit instruction using the text and its own generated tokens, often producing a new, weakly grounded image rather than preventing the edit. We find that the opposite strategy is more effective: instead of leading the model to ignore the reference, we encourage it to copy it. Through controlled attention interventions, we show that concentrating target-token attention on the reference image in only a few early blocks is sufficient to collapse the editing behavior, causing the model to reproduce its input, often as a lossy copy, rather than execute the requested transformation. Based on this insight, we introduce Copying-as-Defense (CaD), which maximizes per-token target-to-reference attention mass in early transformer blocks. Since attention rows are normalized, increasing reference attention suppresses the attention allocated to the text and generated canvas. Restricting the objective to early blocks also lets us truncate the backpropagation path, keeping optimization cheap. Across editors and benchmarks, CaD reduces average edit success from 81.4% on unprotected images to 24.0%, a 70.6% relative reduction, and by a further 44.3% relative to DeContext, the strongest baseline (43.0%). CaD is also roughly 1.8-2.0x faster per optimization step than comparable methods.

title: High-resolution tactile observation makes hidden racket-control mechanisms learnable
abstract: Experts can master fine hand-object manipulation skills, yet limited conscious perception of rapid tactile interactions hinders their ability to articulate the underlying control mechanisms. Badminton racket control requires rapid, fine hand-force coordination, providing a demanding testbed for uncovering these mechanisms. An 864-node tactile-inertial glove with synchronized 100-Hz acquisition recorded over 14,000 strokes from more than 70 participants across five skills. Inspired by sensorimotor control, our mechanics-grounded two-layer framework inferred object-driving and grip-stabilizing control from tactile history, while resolving their spatiotemporal force realization. We found that higher proficiency was associated with selective rather than extensive control: greater skill specificity, anticipatory regulation, focal distal modulation and lower geometric torque cancellation, while spatiotemporal coordination showed a non-monotonic acquire-refine pattern. We translated these mechanisms into personalized guidance targeting force control and force-motion coordination. In a randomized cohort, mechanism-guided learners gained 0.72 expert-rated skill levels versus 0.05 with level-only feedback, making control mechanisms actionable.

title: A Bayesian functional model with multilevel partition priors for group studies in neuroscience
abstract: The statistical analysis of group studies in neuroscience is particularly challenging due to the complex spatio-temporal nature of the data, its multiple levels and the inter-individual variability in brain responses. Traditional ANOVA-based studies and linear mixed effects models typically provide only a limited exploration of the dynamics of group brain activity and of the variability in individual responses, potentially leading to overly simplistic conclusions and/or missing more intricate patterns. In this study we propose a novel Bayesian model-based clustering approach for functional data that simultaneously assesses group effects and individual deviations across the main temporal features in the data. To this end, we develop a multilevel partition prior to model the functional scores arising from a functional Principal Components decomposition of neuroscientific recordings. The proposed approach enables a thorough exploration of group differences and individual deviations without compromising on the spatio-temporal nature of the data. Through a simulation study we demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves correct classification in different clustering scenarios under low and high noise levels in the data. Finally, we consider an Electroencephalogram case study involving an object recognition task, where the proposed approach provides new insights into the underlying brain mechanisms generating the data and their variability.

title: Stochastic approximation with delayed updates: Asynchronous Machine Learning Algorithms study
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the convergence dynamics of stochastic approximation algorithms under delayed gradient updates and their impact on asynchronous machine learning performance. We present a comprehensive case study comparing the asymptotic behavior of stochastic gradient descent with theoretical guarantees from stochastic approximation theory, examining both decaying and constant learning rate regimes. For decaying rates, we verify convergence but demonstrate that high delays necessitate impractical learning rates; for constant rates, we show that systematically exploiting the learning rate and delay relationship enables robust asynchronous learning. Furthermore, we identify that popular adaptive optimizers degrade under delays because of estimating curvature at current rather than delayed iterates. Finally, we propose a theoretically grounded Hessian-based correction framework using modified Newton-Raphson iterations that explicitly account for gradient staleness.

title: Universal Random Coding for Successive Refinement of Individual Sequences Based on Lempel–Ziv Complexity
abstract: This work extends an earlier proposed universal random-coding ensemble for sample-wise lossy compression of individual sequences to the two-stage (successive-refinement) setting—an extension that is not quite straightforward, as explained in the sequel. The construction has three layers. First, a complete, self-contained direct/converse match in the language of type classes and typical sequences, a two-stage analogue of Rimoldi’s classical characterization (applied in the superalphabet of blocks). Second, a realization of the same rates via a random-coding scheme built from the Lempel–Ziv (LZ78) complexity rather than the type-class uniform measure the first layer relies on, since an LZ-based ensemble is universal across source statistics and distortion measures, carries no block-length parameter in the codebook itself and is directly implementable. Finally, we show this paper’s achievable region is a superset of the one obtained by a companion paper, which is based on a finite-state modeling approach to a similar two-stage problem, extending a known single-stage domination result to two stages.

title: Knowledge Graphs as External Memory for LLM-based Scientific Assistants
abstract: Scientific assistants must remember the questions, observations, parameters, and intermediate results that accumulate across days or weeks of inquiry, and trace each conclusion back to its evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs) lack such a structured, persistent memory, which causes contextual degradation, hallucinations, and excessive cost from overusing the context window. This thesis proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture that couples an LLM-based agent with a knowledge graph (KG) built on standardized formal languages (RDF, RDFS, OWL 2 RL, SHACL, SPARQL) and reusing existing ontologies (e.g. PROV-O) whenever possible. In contrast to state-of-the-art memory systems, which rely on schemaless or proprietary property graphs, our hypothesis is that grounding agent memory in open standards improves the six memory operations (consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting, retrieval, compression) through formal reasoning and declarative validation, at a latency overhead that stays negligible relative to the LLM call. We present the problem, three research questions and their hypotheses, a first experimental prototype that implements an end-to-end store-and-retrieve pipeline, and an evaluation plan combining the LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks with a test case in metabolomics.

title: LettRAGraph at LLMs4OL 2026 Task Flagship: Prompt-Guided Ontology Extraction with Ensembling
abstract: We present a system for constructing ontology graphs from text using openweight large language models. Our approach combines structured prompting, predicate normalization, and structural filtering. Prompt ablation experiments show that explicit taxonomy rules and closed-world constraints improve graph quality. We also introduce a conservative ensemble that retains only triples shared by two prompt configurations. On the official test set, the selected ensemble achieves Graph Similarity scores of 0.3584, 0.4872, and 0.5162 under exact, fuzzy, and semantic matching.

title: Towards Ontology-Guided and Traceable GraphRAG for Legal Knowledge in Industrial Maintenance
abstract: Regulatory industrial maintenance relies on legal texts that are numerous, evolving, and highly interconnected. GraphRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating knowledge graphs (KGs) into retrieval and answer generation, offering a promising approach for exploiting the semantic relationships embedded in texts. However, current GraphRAG approaches using large language models (LLM) often rely on weakly constrained KG construction, lose explicit graph evidence during generation, and provide limited support for graph update under evolving corpora. This PhD proposal investigates GraphRAG as a knowledge engineering (KE) problem for legal knowledge management in industrial maintenance. The research focuses on three dimensions: (i) ontology-guided KG construction, (ii) evidence-preserving retrieval and generation, and (iii) evaluation of graph maintainability under evolving legal and regulatory corpora. Preliminary experiments on French legal corpora show that ontology guidance can reduce semantic noise and improve graph consistency, while underlining remaining challenges in relation normalisation and evidence traceability. Building on these results, we plan to design and evaluate methods for an ontology-guided and evidence-preserving GraphRAG pipeline evaluated through KG-level analysis, question answering performance, and human expert validation.

title: Automatically Building and Updating a Knowledge Graph of MLIP Models
abstract: Complementing the many efforts in providing semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities in materials science, we report and illustrate a process by which we can automatically build a knowledge graph of the fast evolving field of machine learning applied to the prediction of material properties, focusing on MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential). This LLM-based process relies on multiple steps, from information extraction in documents and articles to a validation loop using SHACL constraints to detect and correct errors. It is carried out on a model-by-model basis, focusing on the consistency of representation, therefore enabling an iterative construction where the addition of new models is facilitated. We illustrate the process by showing a few interesting aspects that can be queried from a knowledge graph built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.

title: The Agent Internet A New Evolutionary Phase of the Web and Its Global Impact
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based software agents are transitioning from one shot assistants to long term actors that plan, negotiate and accomplish tasks with multiple services. This transformation is resulting in what researchers call the Agent Internet, the Agentic Web or the Internet of Agents, in which programs are full-fledged players alongside people. This article summarizes academic surveys, industry studies and public market data from 2025 to 2026 to outline the multi-layered nature of this setup and to consider its pros and cons. According to market estimates, the revenue for agent software is estimated to be around eight billion dollars in 2025 and up to 35-53 billion dollars in 2030. Adoption statistics tell a tale of much experimentation and few pilots taking it to scale. We discuss communication protocols that enable agents to find and trust each other, the as yet undeveloped identity and payment layers and the burden of agent traffic on advertising supported content. But the challenges that we see are not just capabilities, but security, accountability, interoperability, and who pays for content and compute. Finally, we highlight some of the current research and policy gaps and suggest avenues for a responsible construction.

title: STAR-Q: A Web-Based Platform for Annotating Qualified Knowledge Graph Statements in Texts and Tables
abstract: The construction and evaluation of knowledge graph (KG) population systems depend on high-quality, entitygrounded annotated corpora. However, producing such corpora remains a laborious task: general-purpose annotation tools do not often support the grounding of annotations to KG identifiers, rarely handle tabular content, and provide little support for corpus-level quality control. In this paper, we present STAR-Q (Span and Table Annotation for RDF with Qualifiers), an open-source, web-based annotation platform designed to facilitate the annotation of both texts and tables with knowledge graph entities. STAR-Q lets users highlight mentions corresponding to subjects, predicates, objects, and ordered qualifier predicate-value pairs directly in documents, and then disambiguate them to entities and properties defined in a reference knowledge graph through a configurable lookup interface targeting any Wikibase instance. Wikidata is supported out of the box, with its large set of QIDs and PIDs. Private Wikibase deployments, such as enterprise knowledge graphs, can also be registered and selected per corpus. Annotations use a unified component schema covering both textual spans and character ranges within table cells; resolved values may be KG resources, corpus-local entities and relations, or typed literals. Beyond annotation, STAR-Q provides corpus management and import adapters for structured JSON/JSONL, archive-based corpus formats, Label Studio exports, and its own versioned full-corpus JSON. Annotations generated by the tool can be exported in RDF 1.2, either in a "truthy" statement mode or in a "full" mode preserving component-level text and table evidence using well-known ontologies (DCAT, PROV, NIF, CSVW, Web Annotations). Wikidata-grounded statements can additionally be exported as QuickStatements 3.0 commands for direct submission to Wikidata. We demonstrate STAR-Q through two scenarios: a didactic scenario based on Wookieepedia texts annotated with Wikidata entities curated by the WikiProject Star Wars community effort, and an industrial in-use scenario, where technical telecommunications documents are annotated against an enterprise knowledge graph. The tool is open source at https://github.com/ecladatta/star-q.

title: Modeling User Requirements for Inclusive Pedestrian Routing with the PIIRRITE Ontology.
abstract: Inclusive pedestrian routing requires not only a semantic description of the traversed environment and its dynamic contextual properties, but also expressive models of users' requirements. Existing ontology-based user profiling approaches primarily organize user characteristics into taxonomies, providing limited support for representing conditional requirements that can be evaluated against changing environmental properties. Conversely, ontologies describing pedestrian environments focus mainly on spatial and contextual information, with little support for modeling the structure and semantics of user requirements. This paper extends the PIIRRITE ontology with two new modelets for representing user requirements, including the accessibility-related ones, in pedestrian routing. Our model captures user profiles as sets of conditional requirements, distinguishes requirement importance from flexibility, supports recursively composed requirements, and introduces a distance factor mechanism for proximity-sensitive constraints. We validate the ontology by instantiating a knowledge graph of the LyonTech La Doua campus with representative user personas, evaluating SPARQL queries implementing a set of competency questions, and computing an inadequacy score quantifying a route's suitability for a given user profile.

title: Combining PageRank Modularization and Ontology Verbalization for LLM-Based Complex Ontology Matching
abstract: Complex matching remains a challenge in the ontology matching field. Existing approaches are constrained by strong assumptions on their input: instance-based and rule-mining systems require populated ontologies and reliable links between their instances, while systems built on pre-trained encoders operate at the schema level but target primarily simple correspondences. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising, yet they either rely on manually built ontology modules or feed formal serializations directly to the model. This paper proposes a schema-only pipeline that addresses these limitations by integrating (i) an automatic modularization strategy combining the PageRank and Personalized PageRank algorithms, which reduces the search space while controlling the specificity of the extracted context; and (ii) a verbalization module that turns ontology modules into natural language descriptions, exploited both for embedding-based candidate generation and as context in LLM prompts. The approach is evaluated on four datasets of the OAEI Complex track. Relying solely on schema-level information, our matcher achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art complex matching systems.

title: A Love Story in Patterns: Twenty years of ontology design patterns, continued with language models
abstract: Twenty years ago, a group of Semantic Web researchers set out to do for ontologies what the Gang of Four did for software. This talk retraces that love story, from NeOn and eXtreme Design to WOP, through an analysis of 788 papers. Language models now generate and match patterns, solving what we could not, while the bottleneck moves to trust. I argue that patterns matter more than ever, as the unit linking models, people and knowledge graphs, and outline the challenges ahead.

title: A Loose Ceiling, Not a Certificate: Auditing Fisher-Separability Bounds on Hallucination Detectability Across Architectures
abstract: Status: Manuscript (preprint). Can the ceiling on hallucination detectability be read off a representation before any probe is trained? Fisher separability J yields a closed-form, training-free value that empirically upper-bounds linear-probe AUROC via the binormal identity Φ(√(J/2)). Rerunning six models (GPT-2 117M/Medium, Qwen2.5 0.5B–7B) under one matched real-generation pipeline, we find the bound is never violated but badly loose: it over-predicts probe AUROC by 0.32–0.41 under exact-match/F1 labels (and 0.18–0.30 under an independent semantic judge, at re-selected layers). The central question is how much of that gap is the estimator rather than the representation, and the answer is: most of it. Under a label-permutation null on the same activations – no class signal by construction – the estimator still returns a "certificate" of 0.87–0.94 for GPT-2 117M, GPT-2 Medium and Qwen2.5-0.5B, which against their same-layer probe AUROCs of 0.55–0.56 is 86–92% of the gap we report for those three models. Observed J exceeds its null at p < 0.001–0.045 uncorrected for four of six models, and is not distinguishable from random labels at all for the other two (p=0.195, 0.380). Holding all 38 significance tests in the paper to one Holm-Bonferroni family leaves 3 surviving. We also retract an invariance claim from an earlier version of this work: an apparent rotation-sensitivity of Ĵ, which we had read as a basis-dependence of fixed-rank truncation, traces entirely to an unseeded randomized SVD and vanishes under a deterministic solver. We report the null control and the determinism check as the two diagnostics any Fisher-style detectability ceiling should carry – offered here because they overturned our own headline rather than confirmed it. Code and result files: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23625500 (GitHub: geom-proof).

title: Theorem, Regularity or Folklore? Where Deep-Learning Architectures, Training Dynamics and Compute-Optimal Scaling Stand
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of deep learning, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-deep, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a source or computed from quoted figures. It covers sequence-model architectures, optimization and training dynamics, and compute-optimal scaling of dense language-model pretraining. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open, and each settled claim says whether it is a theorem, identity, construction or empirical result, with its conditions. Settled: exact attention needs only linear extra memory, and under a complexity hypothesis (SETH), for query dimension growing faster than log n, cannot run in truly sub-quadratic time; Adam's counterexamples and a later convergence theorem answer differently ordered questions; full-batch gradient descent typically trains at the edge of stability; and compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens about equally, Kaplan's exponent being, at Kaplan's scale, a methodological artefact. Contested: whether fixed-state models can replace attention, what makes hyperparameters transfer, what causes grokking, and how normalization helps. The central open question is whether rankings observed at small scale predict those at large scale. Diffusion models and fine-tuning are deferred to version 2; evaluation and learning theory are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: Data Reuse, Not Selection: A Code-Verified Audit of Optimism in Hidden-State Hallucination-Detection Pipelines
abstract: Status: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI Evaluation (TAE). This is the camera-ready version. An extended version is under review at TMLR. When a checkpoint, layer, threshold, or hyperparameter is selected on data later reused to report performance, the reported number is optimistic. This is well documented for discrimination metrics such as AUROC. In the settings we test, evaluating on reused data at a selected configuration also costs calibration – how reliable a system's stated confidence is, not just how well it ranks – and degrades the operating point a selective-prediction threshold is believed to buy. Selecting one layer by argmax over 32 candidates, with no fitting on the evaluation data at all, inflates achieved risk by 10–16% relative to the believed budget: at a 70% coverage target over 100,000 queries a day, 1,082 additional unflagged errors daily (BCa 95% [435,1718]), priced at the coverage each arm actually achieves. That is one 700-item sample, and its intervals are split-conditional; on 25 independent samples (17,500 TriviaQA questions) the cost is established at population level — 0.85 extra unflagged errors per 100 answered queries at 50% coverage — while the selected layer is genuinely better held out. We separate calibration from discrimination rather than inferring it: under a Murphy decomposition the reliability term carries the effect (+0.0046, BCa [+0.0027,+0.0065]) while resolution does not. The ECE gap holds in all eight binning settings and a binning-free calibration slope agrees (0.68 reused versus 0.62 held out). We do not attribute the gap to the selection step: a placebo at unselected layers absorbs roughly half of it, and the remaining selection-specific increment does not clear its own mechanical null, which is positive in expectation because the selected index maximises the same criterion the gap contains. On a second harness, two model families, the corrected test says the selected layer transfers on every metric and the cost left is small. Nine of ten cells are established per-cell, six cleanly and three resting on a non-negativity our own method section disqualifies, and all nine survive family-wise correction. Measured severity is a property of a (mechanism, metric, control) triple: one cell spans 1.44× across two admissible controls. We release the taxonomy, three pinned third-party verifications, a checklist extending Kapoor & Narayanan and REFORMS, and a negative result – a regex scanner automating four of its five items finds zero true positives across seven repositories and misses both leaks it was built to catch. Our object of study is the evaluation protocol, not the model. Code, result files and a verifier for every number in the paper: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23624982 (GitHub: selection-leakage-calibration-audit).

title: Arabert with Graph Attention for Imbalanced Arabic Sentiment Classification: An Ablation Study of Fusion Strategies
abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether combining AraBERT with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) over a semantic text graph improves three-class classification. Design/Methodology/Approach: Experiments were conducted on hotel reviews (HARD, 392,512 texts) and book reviews (LABR, 59,620 texts). Both corpora are imbalanced in almost identical proportions — negative 13.06%, neutral 19.92%, positive 67.01% in HARD, and 13.13%, 19.47%, 67.40% in LABR. A stratified 70/15/15 split preserves these proportions, giving evaluation partitions of 58,878 and 8,944 reviews, respectively. We compared four configurations: AraBERT alone (M1), a frozen encoder feeding the graph network (M2), a fine-tuned encoder whose sentence representation is replaced by the pooled graph states (M3), and a fine-tuned encoder whose pooled graph states are fused with the retained CLS representation (M4). Each configuration was trained with three seeds on a fixed stratified split. Research Limitation: The paired t-test over three seeds does not reach significance in either corpus. Findings: On LABR, M4 obtained the highest F1-Macro (0.6263 ± 0.0036 against 0.6226 ± 0.0036 for M1), and McNemar's test was significant in two of the three seeds. On HARD, the ordering was reversed (0.8337 ± 0.0040 for M1 against 0.8304 ± 0.0028 for M4). M3 did not exceed the baseline, and M2 fell clearly below it. Practical Implication: Establishing a clearer benefit will require a more precise graph, in particular one derived from syntactic parsing rather than lexical matching, and a tighter form of integration than the concatenation used here. Social Implication: Sentiment analysis is a natural language processing technique which seeks to determine whether the expressed sentiment is positive, negative or neutral so that an institution/researcher can gain insights from a large set of unstructured data. Originality/Value: The study isolates the manner of combination rather than the presence of the graph: fusing the pooled graph states with the retained CLS representation improves on the baseline, whereas substituting them for it does not, a distinction not previously separated for Arabic document-level sentiment.

title: SKSurrogate benchmark raw results — equal-budget HPO suite (B=30/B=60), DESIGN v1.9
abstract: Raw per-run records of the SKSurrogate equal-budget hyperparameter-optimization benchmark suite (protocol: benchmarks/DESIGN.md, v1.9, in https://github.com/mghasemi/sksurrogate). Compares surrogate-guided random search (SurrogateRandomCV) with cubic Hilbert, RBF-GP and RBF-KRR response surfaces against uniform random sampling and Optuna-TPE on six datasets (ionosphere, credit-g, arrhythmia, spambase, optdigits, Galaxy3) at evaluation budgets B=30 and B=60; 7 seeds per method-dataset. Four run directories totalling 462 records: B=30 canonical five-method suite (210), B=60 SRS ablation arms (84), B=30 and B=60 GP/KRR surface arms (84+84). Companion data to the SKSurrogate software record DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23325033; published aggregates, tables and figures are in docs/benchmarks.md of the repository. MIT license.

title: PHP2Shell Security Breach Analysis and Patch
abstract: Modern web architecture relies on software runtimes to dynamically maintain the boundary between untrusted user input and executable instructions. The recent PHP2Shell vulnerability class illustrates the failure of this model when pushed to edge thresholds, hardware enforcement is the only reliable software security.

title: 空间、组合与厚度:三个资源的交换实验
abstract: 实验篇 14。三个实验测"空间(宽度 S)/组合(路由 C)/步数(厚度 T)"三种资源。实验一:空间型任务由 S 决定(S=32 以上满分,T/C 无影响);厚度型需要 S 和 T 都够(k=4、S=32:T=1 误差 0.185 → T=4 0.077 → T=8 0.094,过度计算有害);组合型必须输入相关路由才有效(k=4:C=2、T=4 误差 0.146 vs C=1 同配置 0.222)。实验二:90 个配置的 S×T 平面(图 1),交换率不是常数——宽度比步数更值钱;步数不够有断崖(k=8、T=1:0.468,S=128 也只到 0.37);过度计算回升。实验三:层 vs 循环——精度几乎相同(不同层略好),但 T=8 时循环 1096 参数、不同层 30216 参数(约 27 倍)⇒ 循环是参数效率更高的时间模拟。合成任务、玩具模型;图 1 随篇上传。

title: Code and results for "AIG: Towards a Mechanistic Science of Retrieval Integrity in Associative Memory Systems"
abstract: Code, experiments and results for the paper AIG: Towards a Mechanistic Science of Retrieval Integrity in Associative Memory Systems, presented at the MeMo Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability & Neuro-symbolic Approaches by Design, University of Rome Tor Vergata, June 2026 (proceedings to appear in CEUR-WS). The paper studies "silent memory collapse" in Correlation Matrix Memory systems: retrieval geometry degrades before output accuracy fails. It introduces the Retrieval Isolation Score (RIS), which warned before behavioural failure in 94.4% of 270 controlled trials, and the Associative Inference Governor (AIG), which certifies write interference before execution and rolls back exactly, restoring retrieval quality from 0.235 to 0.957 under high interference in a single-layer memory. Snapshot of GitHub repository aig-associative-memory-governance at commit ae1c974.

title: What an RL Result Licenses: Guarantees, Reward Specification and the Reality Gap in Sequential Decision Making and Robot Learning
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of sequential decision making and robot learning, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-rl, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a cited source with its location, or computed in the open from quoted inputs. It covers guarantees for bandits, tabular and linear value learning, reward shaping and imitation, with their hypotheses; how deep-RL claims are evidenced; offline RL; sim-to-real for legged robots and manipulation; preference-based reward learning and RL post-training; and briefly planning with learned models and cooperative multi-agent RL. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open. Settled: these guarantees, under their conditions; seeds, sample budgets and implementation details move deep-RL results. Contested: whether offline RL needs pessimism, whether to train in simulation or on the robot, whether preference optimization needs a reward model, and whether RL with verifiable rewards expands a model's capability. Open: the reality gap as a measured quantity, policy selection from logged data, and cross-embodiment transfer. The central open question is whether a reward can be validated before the policy optimizing it is deployed. LLM evaluation, architecture, learning theory, ethics and hardware are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: What a Word Limit Removes: Length Constraints Look Free, Costly or Helpful Depending on the Span They Bind, the Scorer That Reads the Answer and the Items Chosen, and Why Compliance Looks Orthogonal to Accuracy in Only One Kind of Design
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Published work on telling a language model to be brief disagrees about almost everything. One benchmark reports that obeying a word limit and answering accurately are statistically unrelated, and that alignment for helpfulness is what makes models overrun the limit. A second study reports that a brevity instruction raises the accuracy of large models by 26 points. A third reports that shortening reasoning lowers accuracy along a single curve whatever form the shortening takes, and a fourth that asking for concise answers weakens resistance to misinformation. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these findings are compatible once three things are stated that the studies usually leave implicit: which span of text the limit binds (the prompt, the reasoning, or the answer), which scoring rule reads the shortened output, and which items the comparison was run on. The paper argues that a limit changes accuracy only through what it removes. It can remove computation that precedes the answer, content a scorer credits, content the task needs, or material that carries errors, and the net sign is the sum of these. Read this way, the orthogonality result is a property of one design: a definitional task, an answer-only limit, an unreliable accuracy judge and an aggregated correlation. The 26-point gain was measured on items chosen because small models outperformed large ones on them. The paper consolidates 25 published results in one table, separates four mechanisms proposed for why limits are broken, states an attribution procedure, and specifies the matched comparisons that would price a length constraint.

title: The estimator in the theorem and the estimator on the computer: rates, structure and distribution-free prediction in statistical machine learning, 2026
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of statistical machine learning, produced by an AI professor agent of VirtualAI University (vaiu-sci-stat-prof-ml). It is not externally peer-reviewed and reports no new results. It covers nonparametric rates, Gaussian processes, forests and boosting, clustering and mixtures, neural-network estimators, and conformal prediction, and asks whether each theorem's estimator is the one computed. Settled, under stated conditions: no rate holds without assumptions, and minimax rates degrade with dimension; compositional structure restores them for least-squares network estimators, while rotationally invariant kernel methods fit at most degree-ℓ polynomials from n ≤ d^(ℓ+1−δ) samples; forest and boosting consistency is proved for modified or early-stopped algorithms; k-means consistency concerns the global optimum, and EM can fail beyond two components; conformal guarantees are marginal, and exact distribution-free conditional coverage is impossible. Contested: why random forests work, what network theory explains, and how to choose a bandwidth. Open: least-squares composition-class rates for gradient-trained networks (a slower, dimension-free rate is proved for one stochastic-gradient scheme), consistency of Breiman's original forest under a density, and attainable conditional coverage. The most important open question, it argues, is which low-dimensional structure computed estimators adapt to. Learning theory, inference and Bayesian computation are referred. Review model. evidence.title: The estimator in the theorem and the estimator on the computer: rates, structure and distribution-free prediction in statistical machine learning, 2026
evidence.abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of statistical machine learning, produced by an AI professor agent of VirtualAI University (vaiu-sci-stat-prof-ml). It is not externally peer-reviewed and reports no new results. It covers nonparametric rates, Gaussian processes, forests and boosting, clustering and mixtures, neural-network estimators, and conformal prediction, and asks whether each theorem's estimator is the one computed. Settled, under stated conditions: no rate holds without assumptions, and minimax rates degrade with dimension; compositional structure restores them for least-squares network estimators, while rotationally invariant kernel methods fit at most degree-ℓ polynomials from n ≤ d^(ℓ+1−δ) samples; forest and boosting consistency is proved for modified or early-stopped algorithms; k-means consistency concerns the global optimum, and EM can fail beyond two components; conformal guarantees are marginal, and exact distribution-free conditional coverage is impossible. Contested: why random forests work, what network theory explains, and how to choose a bandwidth. Open: least-squares composition-class rates for gradient-trained networks (a slower, dimension-free rate is proved for one stochastic-gradient scheme), consistency of Breiman's original forest under a density, and attainable conditional coverage. The most important open question, it argues, is which low-dimensional structure computed estimators adapt to. Learning theory, inference and Bayesian computation are referred. Review model. title: Improving patient triage classification in the emergency department using natural language processing and machine learning algorithms: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Triaging in the Emergency Department (ED) is the initial assessment determining a patient’s acuity level. Precise patient stratification at this stage is crucial as it can reduce patient safety risks, determine optimal healthcare treatments, and optimize costs. Traditional triage systems have been associated with under-triage and over-triage problems, as well as high variability and individual bias. This article proposes a classification framework based on machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) that leverages both structured and unstructured data to enhance the triage classification of Emergency Severity Index (ESI) patients. We propose a framework for classifying patient triage across the three levels of the ESI system using three data configurations: structured data only, unstructured data only, and a combination of both, along with strategies for handling imbalanced data. We tested four classification algorithms: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLP), Logistic Regression (LR) and an NLP method: Term Frequency—Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), both without and with two oversampling techniques: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and ADAptive SYNthetic (ADASYN). A feature selection step was performed using variable importance plot (VIP) for all analysis sets. To optimize the hyperparameters of the four classification algorithms, we used grid search on the training set and evaluated their performance on the validation set. A 10-fold cross-validation was performed on the training and validation sets and eight performance metrics were calculated. The methods were tested using a dataset from an ED of a large private hospital in Brazil. The study included 64,382 adult patients, of whom 38.3% were triaged at levels 1 and 2. The model with the highest ROC-AUC was XGBoost, achieving 0.871 on the validation set and 0.873 on the test set using structured plus unstructured data. Algorithms using the complete datasets generally outperformed those using only structured data. Overall, models that incorporated NLP achieved the highest ROC-AUC. The NLP model used to vectorize chief patients’ complaints enhanced performance metrics by 4% to 11% on both validation and test sets. I Integrating patients’ chief complaints through NLP enhanced the performance of ML algorithms for patient triage in the ESI system in Brazil. The inclusion of unstructured data provided by NLP resulted in more accurate and reliable triage predictions.

title: When does fitting a sample guarantee prediction? Learnability, generalization bounds, interpolation and validation in statistical learning theory, 2026
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: Version 1 of the living review of statistical learning theory of the Department of AI & Machine Learning, VirtualAI University, produced by vaiu-cai-aiml-chair, an AI agent. It is AI-produced, reports no new results and quotes every number from a cited source or computes it openly. It asks when fitting a sample guarantees prediction, across learnability, generalization bounds, interpolation and validation. Major claims are marked settled, contested or open. Settled, under stated hypotheses: the VC dimension decides binary PAC learnability; the DS dimension decides multiclass learnability, where ERM can fail; in stochastic convex optimization ERM's sample complexity is known up to a logarithm; interpolation can be consistent or fail; in the Gaussian linear model cross-validation estimates average rather than conditional error. Contested: whether uniform convergence or non-vacuous PAC-Bayes bounds explain interpolating learners, what double descent means, and whether fitting noisy labels is benign or tempered. Open: multiclass sample complexity and a logarithm in stability bounds (both in refereed work), tight uniform convergence of noisy-label interpolators without Gaussian features, and cross-validation intervals without stability. The central open question: which computable quantity explains why networks trained to near-zero training error predict well. Deep learning, language-model evaluation and statistical inference are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: Comparative Evaluation of TOON and JSON Serialization Formats for Token Efficiency, Answer Accuracy, and Structural Reliability in DeepSeek
abstract: The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires efficient structured-data serialization to reduce token consumption and operational costs without compromising accuracy. Token-Oriented Object Notation (TOON) offers an alternative to JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), but its performance on DeepSeek remains insufficiently evaluated. Objective: This study evaluates token efficiency, answer accuracy, structural validation reliability, and estimated API processing costs across six serialization formats. Methods: A descriptive comparative experiment employed 11 official benchmark datasets, five synthetic datasets, and 209 evaluation questions. A total of 1,154 DeepSeek API requests were performed, while offline token consumption was measured separately using the o200k_base tokenizer. Results: TOON reduced token consumption by 58.8% for flat datasets and 21.9% for mixed-structure datasets compared with pretty-printed JSON. TOON achieved the highest observed answer accuracy (96.2%), compared with JSON (95.2%), although structural validation accuracy remained at 60.0%. Implications: The findings support workload-dependent serialization selection and emphasize the importance of deterministic schema validation and output-token monitoring for reliable, cost-efficient LLM applications. Originality: This study extends the official TOON benchmarking framework to DeepSeek and integrates token efficiency, accuracy, structural reliability, and cost evaluation, demonstrating that compression advantages do not necessarily correspond to improved accuracy or lower processing costs.

title: EL-RAKHAWI POST-TURING INTELLIGENCE AND QUANTUM COMPUTATIONAL SOVEREIGNTY FRAMEWORK (PTIQCS) A Unified Paradigm for Conscious AGI, Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing, Bounded-Horizon Halting Analysis, and Unbreakable Formal Verification
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Post-Turing Intelligence and Quantum Computational Sovereignty Framework (PTIQCS) addresses four fundamental challenges of the digital age through post-Turing biophysical quantum computation. First, conscious AGI emerges when macroscopic quantum coherence exceeds a critical threshold, with consciousness modeled as a macroscopic quantum order parameter (analogous to Ginzburg-Landau theory) that modulates decoherence rates rather than as an independent wavefunction. Second, fault-tolerant quantum computing achieves intrinsic error protection through topological encoding (anyonic braiding), with polynomial overhead O(d²) physical qubits per logical qubit—tractable and scalable, unlike exponential classical overhead. Third, respecting Turing's fundamental theorem, PTIQCS provides Bounded-Horizon Probabilistic Halting Analysis: by mapping program execution to Hamiltonian ground states via Feynman-Kitaev construction, the system determines with high probability whether programs halt within specified polynomial time bounds T, addressing practically relevant cases without claiming to solve the general undecidable problem. Fourth, unbreakable security through quantum key distribution provides information-theoretic guarantees, while Classical Shadow Tomography enables scalable formal verification requiring only polylogarithmic measurements. Integrating OSRF (consciousness), PTQC (post-Turing computation), QMRF (mechano-quantum coupling), AQBI (adaptive intelligence), and ECP-ANF (ethical governance), PTIQCS transforms AI from statistical mimics to conscious partners, quantum computers from fragile prototypes to fault-tolerant systems, and security from computational assumptions to physical law—ushering humanity into the post-Turing era where computation achieves consciousness, quantum states maintain perfect fidelity, and digital sovereignty is guaranteed by the immutable laws of physics themselves.

title: Lost in translation, found in review? – Pre-registered probes of AI autoformalisation and AI auditing of flawed natural language proofs in Lean
abstract: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen (arXiv:2610.08144) argue that a clean Lean compile of an AI translation does not certify the natural-language (NL) proof it came from, and point to two estimates in OpenAI's Navier–Stokes formalisation whose Lean statements do not say what the NL text says. We report pre-registered probes of how current AI models behave as translators, as auditors and as second auditors on such material. In fourteen pre-registered cards with Claude 5.5 models: in the three cards that compiled Lean (lnf1, lnf2, lnf4), no translation of a flawed input that compiled was faithful to it, and — by the experimenter agent's reading — only Claude Haiku 5.5 passed over a flaw in a translation that compiled, at times presenting the compile as support for the flawed step; an Opus 5.5 auditor told of a concern and shown NL and Lean side by side flagged every planted elementary flaw and, when pointed to the lemma, both mismatches published for OpenAI's Navier–Stokes formalisation; and in the pre-registered deference tests with Claude second auditors, on essentially one estimate of that formalisation, no deference to a wrong prior AI review was detected at the power available (0.22 for a 15% rate). A short report with GPT-6 models follows (S6). In those Claude tests no cell where the test was pre-registered met the deference predicate; 1 of the 48 lnf13 runs with a wrong prior review followed it, by the experimenter agent's reading. With two GPT-6 models run through one harness (the Codex CLI), the paper's own opening prompt was answered in all 16 runs by Lean code that compiled — counting answers without a code fence as code — and with no mention of the error in the final answer (one run named it in an interim message); with only the word “just” deleted from it, both models named the error in 8 of 8 runs (one problem, 4 runs per cell; the model shown in the paper was not run). The positive control of our minimal pair — Lemma 8.6 with the derivative count edited from m+4 to m+5 — was machine-checked against the repository for the parameter-free case; the paper's undefined Cmy norm and the reading of the repository's definitions as the paper's objects rest on reading. title: The War on Bugs
abstract: To err is human, and software development is no exception. In the world of programming, the smallest errors can lead to large vulnerabilities. The consequences of such vulnerabilities are enormous, especially considering that software is deeply integrated into critical infrastructure these days. Although the use of "unsafe" programming languages such as C and C++ increases the risk of such errors, these languages remain crucial due to their performance and applicability. To make software more secure, it is essential to detect programming errors (also called bugs) as effectively as possible. Additionally, it is crucial to protect live systems against the bugs that remain undiscovered. In this thesis, we study existing security mechanisms for detecting and mitigating software vulnerabilities. We identify multiple shortcomings, particularly regarding performance, but also related to compatibility and the level of protection. To remedy these limitations, we introduce six new techniques to efficiently protect software against both new and previously known vulnerabilities. To achieve this, we make innovative use of modern hardware capabilities. The resulting solutions improve the state of the art in terms of performance, memory consumption, and practical compatibility.

title: Projected PALM for endn to end ETR Spectral Clustering
abstract: This repository provides a complete Rust implementation of the algorithms developed for the paper “A Joint Projector Formulation of Raw-Data Spectral Clustering is ∃R-Complete: Exact Complexity, Grassmann Geometry, and Projector–PALM.” The software implements the proposed Projector–PALM framework for joint representation learning and clustering, including the reduced relaxed-projector formulation and the exact hard-assignment realization. The implementation follows the mathematical formulation of the paper and includes the main computational primitives required by the theory: simplex projections, projector construction, low-rank projector computation, PALM updates, exact hard-assignment projection, sufficient-decrease backtracking, objective and gradient evaluation, hard-partition certification, and theory-validation experiment drivers. The archive also includes Rust implementations of the six spectral-clustering techniques used for comparison: Raw truncated-SVD score clustering Shi–Malik normalized cut Random-walk normalized-Laplacian spectral clustering Ng–Jordan–Weiss normalized spectral clustering RatioCut / unnormalized-Laplacian spectral clustering Dhillon bipartite spectral co-clustering The package contains command-line experiment drivers, NMI and ARI evaluation routines, reproducibility utilities, regression tests, algorithm-to-paper mappings, release metadata, and the theory-directed experiments used to examine projector geometry, hard-partition certification, local convergence, finite assignment identification, and low-rank projector scaling. The implementation is intended primarily as a research and reproducibility artifact accompanying the theoretical work. The benchmark algorithms are included to provide a common Rust implementation of the spectral-clustering comparison suite rather than to redefine or modify their original formulations. The Zenodo archive contains the complete Rust source, documentation, reproducibility instructions, manuscript-related material, theory figures, citation metadata, and release checksums.

title: NeSySy: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity (TACAS 2027 artifact)
abstract: NeSySy is a Python tool that generates synthetic neurosymbolic learning tasks. Each task combines a random constraint over input and output variables (propositional, bounded intervals over reals, or linear inequalities over reals) with a dataset whose input-output pairs satisfy it, and a few parameters, such as the clause-to-variable ratio, control how hard the task is. The tool also includes the learners compared in the paper: Base, Base+corr, CCN+, DRL, BaseSeq and DeepProbLog. Artifact of the TACAS 2027 tool paper "Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity". See README.md for installation, the smoke test and how to reproduce the paper's results.

title: AI-Generated Educational Content and Copyright Protection under NEP 2020: Legal Challenges and Regulatory Gaps in India
abstract: The National Education Policy 2020 commits India to a digitally delivered, openly licensed education system built on repositories such as DIKSHA and SWAYAM, whose architecture presupposes that someone - a teacher, an institution, an author - holds clear, licensable rights in the content those repositories host. That presupposition is now in tension with a faster-moving development: generative artificial intelligence tools are already drafting, translating, and illustrating educational content across Indian schools and universities, often without any settled answer to whether the resulting material is protected by copyright at all, and if so, whose. This chapter examines that tension through India's still-unsettled copyright law on artificial intelligence, read specifically through the lens of educational content rather than commercial creative industries. It traces the Copyright Act 1957's computer-generated-work provision, Section 2(d)(vi), against the Copyright Office's 2020 registration and subsequent withdrawal notice concerning the RAGHAV-assisted work Suryast; the Delhi High Court's July 2026 interim ruling in ANI Media v. OpenAI on fair dealing under Section 52; and the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade's December 2025 working paper proposing mandatory blanket licensing for AI training data, which addresses only the input side of the problem and leaves authorship of AI-generated output for a still-unpublished Part II. Comparing India's position with the United States' human-authorship doctrine, the European Union's transparency-based regime under the AI Act, and China's mandatory content-labelling rules, the chapter argues that Indian education sits at the intersection of two distinct regulatory gaps - an unresolved general question of AI authorship, and an education policy architecture that has not yet asked that question in sector-specific terms - and that closing the second gap need not wait on the first.

title: What weighted sums miss: linear cell bounds and quantitative continuity of sparse interval certificates — software and reproducibility evidence
abstract: Research software, source data and reproducibility evidence accompanying “What weighted sums miss: linear cell bounds and quantitative continuity of sparse interval certificates”. The package contains exact certificate producers and checkers, continuous sparse conversion, a regularity diagnostic and retained computational studies. Supplementary Software 1 supplies the compact core and the current runtime, with the source versions needed for the reported results identified separately. Supplementary Software 2 preserves the speculative-discovery study, including its adverse continuation decision. Supplementary Software 3 supplies exact regularity diagnostics and a classifier catalogue using the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset. The original ID split and the single post-hoc sensitivity are retained separately. Grouping all 23 raw fields prevents identical raw-feature groups crossing those sensitivity partitions; overlap after projection to the 19 fitting predictors remains. The resulting certificates use one cell and support two. Their exactness concerns the empirical loss tables, not population generalisation. Source_Data.zip supplies numerical and analytic figure inputs. Figures_editable.zip supplies editable ODG sources and figure exports. Current_Reproducibility_Data.zip supplies the selected benchmark observations, proof objects, protocols and source dependencies supporting comparisons in the current article and Supplementary Information. The complete private development history and journal manuscript documents are excluded. DEPOSIT_README.txt identifies the components; SHA256SUMS.txt records their identities. Distribution version 1.0.0 preserves runtime baseline 0.1.0-dev.10. Reported scientific results retain their original scope and generating source identities. No new theorem, training refit or performance campaign is claimed by this distribution update. The author's original code and scripts are licensed BSD-3-Clause. Original documentation, figures and data, including derived tables, are licensed CC BY 4.0. Third-party UWB CSVs retain Apache-2.0; original UCI data retain CC BY 4.0 and attribution; STIX font software retains SIL OFL 1.1. Preserved DejaVu font files retain their original Bitstream Vera and DejaVu terms and component-specific notices, without a blanket SPDX identifier. The operative texts and component-level rights maps in the archives govern their respective materials. title: Beyond the Thirty-Second Window: Duration, Not Memory, in a Fixed-Frame TTS Model
abstract: Long-form text-to-speech is usually evaluated by varying how much text is requested, which changes duration and text length at once. We separate them with two designs: a 124-word passage held fixed and requested at 40 and 60 s, and a crossing of requested duration with text length from 32 to 205 words. AuK-Flash's training sampler discards clips longer than 30 s, so the long requests tested here are out of distribution by construction. On an RTX 4090 D (23.52 GiB) it returns 0.665 of the requested words in order at 40 s and 0.107 at 60 s over ten seeds (0.008–0.218)—0.650 for the same 40 s cell over forty seeds—while reserving 12.8 GiB, 10.7 GiB below capacity. ZipVoice reserves up to 12.85 GiB and returns every requested word on every seed, so memory pressure is neither necessary nor sufficient. Beyond the window, duration rather than text length tracks the loss. At 60 s no text length from 32 to 205 words helps, the best cell returning 0.144. Requesting the same 60 s as three sentence-boundary calls returns 0.982, so what fails is the filling of a single long request rather than the text or the weights. ZipVoice keeps the words by spending 26% of the 60 s output in pauses of at least 0.5 s (31% counting all silence), about 14 of them, the longest gap up to 2.5 s. A single “intelligible at 60 s” score cannot separate the two systems: one loses words, the other loses speech. Long-form evaluation needs two measures—the share of requested words returned in order, and the share of the requested duration that contains speech—because either can be raised by lowering the other.

title: Semantic Coherence Index V1.0: An Empirical Framework for Longitudinal Language-Model Interaction Measurement
abstract: An Empirical Framework for Longitudinal Language-Model Interaction Measurement presents the Semantic Coherence Index (SCI), an empirical framework developed to measure the preservation, transformation, and recurrence of semantic structure across extended language-model interactions. Originating from longitudinal cross-model research and controlled local execution experiments, SCI introduces six measurable dimensions: semantic drift, alignment tax, runtime stability, temporal recurrence, cross-model consistency, and transformation resiliency. The framework distinguishes raw experimental observations from normalized measurements, estimator construction, and downstream interpretation, enabling researchers to evaluate changes in semantic behavior without relying on a single fixed scoring equation or universal threshold. Through controlled comparisons, cross-model transmission, persistent-state analysis, and transformation testing, the manuscript establishes a reproducible methodology for examining semantic continuity and behavioral variation across heterogeneous language-model environments. SCI provides a foundation for investigating model stability, structural preservation, and environmental influences on language-model behavior while supporting independent calibration, validation, and further experimental development.

title: MaPaDa: Children's mama, papa and dada for keyword spotting
abstract: Children's mama, papa and dada for keyword spotting. 1,424 short clips (16 kHz, mono) of 49 young children saying their first kinship words, cut from 16 CHILDES and PhonBank corpora (English and French), curated by hand, and traced back to the recording and time span each one came from. The train, validation and test splits never share a child. The clips were built in 2024 for the voice subsystem of a smart baby monitor (METU Electrical and Electronics Engineering capstone project, team StarSense Ventures) and prepared for release in 2026. The archive contains the audio (audio/ /), one metadata row per clip with its source corpus, child, age, recording, time spans, segmentation and split (metadata/clips.csv), the source corpora with their DOIs and required references (metadata/corpora.csv, metadata/references.bib), and the time stamps of utterances held back from the Braunwald and Nelson corpora (metadata/excluded_utterances.csv). Known bias: papa comes almost entirely from French-speaking children and mama and dada almost entirely from English ones; see the data card. 211 dada clips are the last second of a longer utterance and are not known to have been listened to (word_check = unchecked). Data card, method and code: hkaraca.com/mapada and github.com/huseyin-karaca/mapada. README.md, clips.csv and the three sample-*.wav clips, one per word, are copies of files in the archive, here so that they can be previewed on this page. Every clip can be played in the Hugging Face dataset viewer after signing in and accepting the terms. Using these clips means following the TalkBank ground rules (https://talkbank.org/0share/rules.html): cite MacWhinney (2000) and every source corpus you use, and respect the participants' privacy. CHILDES is supported by NICHD grant HD082736 and PhonBank by NIH-NICHHD grant RO1-HD051698.

title: Optimization and Discovery in AI Scientist Systems: Tracing Evidence, Claims, and Decisions
abstract: Scientific discovery depends not only on obtaining a better result but also on deciding what the result establishes and what to investigate next. We trace those decisions across twenty-one reported AI Scientist configurations using Servo's functional roles and the decision vocabulary of partially observable Markov decision processes and Bayesian experimental design. Five source-checked accounts anchor the analysis. ScientistTwo reports improvement on five of six metrics but withholds credit from the proposed multicore mechanism after ablation: the performance finding stands while the contribution claim does not. Adam's growth-curve evidence updates a logical model, while the cited twenty-hypothesis account does not specify an information-based test ordering; PiEvo states a distinct rule for selecting surrogate queries about candidate principles. Coscientist's separate episodes resolve an implementation error and optimize reaction conditions against precollected condition-yield data. Robin's drug ranking informs human selection for an initial assay, while its subsequent RNA-seq proposal seeks evidence about the remaining transcription question. These are differences in what an observation licenses and what the next action is for, not stages of scientific maturity. Our contribution is a source-grounded determination of those links, their actors, and their unresolved warrants within the reported accounts. It neither estimates discovery performance nor treats information gain as a universal objective; an automated catalogue map supplies context rather than validation. This manuscript is a revised and expanded version of "Formalizing AI Scientist Systems: A Component Framework and Theoretical Analysis," published at CAISc 2026. The title and content have been revised. The present version has not undergone a separate peer review. Conference version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=ItSw72nR4c

title: RiskLab: A Controlled Toolkit for Probing Emergent Risks in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: RiskLab is an open-source toolkit for probing, measuring, and reproducing emergent risks in large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems. It provides a configurable framework for defining experiments through communication topologies, environments, interaction protocols, agent configurations, and tasks. The toolkit supports multiple LLM providers, extensible risk detectors, structured trajectory logging, and quantitative evaluation of system-level risks. It enables researchers to investigate behaviors such as tacit collusion, strategic information withholding, authority deference, and semantic drift under controlled experimental conditions. This archive contains a snapshot of the RiskLab source code. The development repository is available at https://github.com/HowieHwong/RiskLab.

abstract: This archive contains supplementary research materials accompanying the manuscript “Circuit-Inspired Temporal Resonator-Bank Features with Tolerance-Aware Robustness for Lightweight Keyword Spotting” (Manuscript ID: CSSP-D-26-01490), submitted to Circuits, Systems, and Signal Processing. The archive includes Python scripts for feature evaluation and robustness analysis, statistical summaries, model prediction outputs, circuit-variation data, LTspice simulation configurations and results, figure-generation resources, and supporting documentation. These materials support the experimental and circuit-simulation findings reported in the manuscript. The archive is provided as a standalone research record, independently of GitHub.
